bread-french-or-vienna-whole-wheat-toast.title: Bread, French or Vienna, whole wheat, toasted

content.title: About
content.content: French or Vienna whole‑wheat bread, toasted to a golden crust, is a traditional loaf made from whole wheat flour. It has a dense yet airy crumb, a mildly tangy flavor, and a fragrant, crunchy crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The French baguette and Viennese loaf have centuries‑old origins in medieval bakeries.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crisp crust while keeping the interior soft.
Whole‑wheat versions retain bran and germ, boosting nutritional value compared with white bread.
In Hungary, the bread is often baked in a steam oven, giving the crust a characteristic shine.
In some French regions, toasted bread is served with olive oil and cheese as a snack.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑wheat bread provides soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Whole grains supply iron, magnesium, and zinc, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact after toasting
items.content: Toasting slows carbohydrate absorption, helping to moderate glucose spikes.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, healthy fats, and fiber helps you feel full longer.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The bread contains gluten and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties can be salty; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Toasted bread has slightly higher calories due to reduced moisture.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: A wheat allergy can cause reactions in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted whole‑wheat bread works well for sandwiches, avocado toast, soups, and salads. Spread with low‑fat cheese, nut butter, or use as a base for croutons.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and reheat in a toaster.

chicken-thigh-fried-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is dark‑meat from the upper leg of a chicken, known for its rich flavor and higher fat content than breast meat. When fried in a coating, a crispy crust forms, but in this product the skin and coating are not consumed and serve only as a cooking medium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more iron and zinc than breast meat.
Frying in a coating raises the calorie count by roughly 30 % compared with plain meat.
In many cuisines, thighs are traditionally breaded with flour, egg, and spices before frying.
A properly fried crust locks in juices, keeping the meat moist.
Chicken is one of the most affordable high‑quality protein sources worldwide.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B6, niacin, and riboflavin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Iron, zinc, and phosphorus in the meat contribute to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium and vitamin B6 help maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: The fat in thigh meat offers sustained satiety and a steady energy source.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying adds saturated fats, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may react to chicken proteins.

items.title: Cooking contaminants
items.content: Overheating oil can produce harmful compounds such as acrylamide; fry at moderate temperatures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fried thigh hot, cutting it into bite‑size pieces. Remove the skin and coating before eating if desired. Pair with vegetables, potatoes, or a fresh salad. Light sauces—yogurt‑based, tomato, or herb—enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw thighs refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked pieces store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Discard if an off‑smell or slimy texture develops.

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog is a ready‑to‑eat sausage product, usually made from beef, pork or poultry, placed in a long bun. It is commonly served with mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise and various toppings such as cheese, onions or sauerkraut.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
The term “hot dog” originated from a joke that the sausage might contain “dogs”.
Americans consume more than 20 million hot dogs per day, especially on Independence Day.
There are over 200 different topping and sauce variations, from classic mustard to exotic chili, pineapple, and cheese sauces.
In some countries, like Japan, hot dogs are served as rice‑wrapped “rolls”.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The meat in a hot dog provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hot dogs contain B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates in the bun delivers quick energy.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: Easy to transport and eat, making it a popular street‑food item.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Large amounts of saturated fat can raise cholesterol levels when consumed frequently.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Hot dogs often contain high sodium and nitrites, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to meat or additives
items.content: Some individuals may react to spices, sauces or additives used in the sausage.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One hot dog can contain 250–400 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Thermal safety
items.content: Insufficiently heated products may harbor pathogenic bacteria such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot dogs are usually heated on a grill, in an oven or microwave, then placed in a split bun and topped with sauces, vegetables and seasonings to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hot dogs in the refrigerator at ≤ 4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen versions can be kept for up to 2 months. Heat thoroughly before consumption.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-seafood-ready.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Seafood (Ready-to-Heat)

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and seafood is a ready‑to‑heat meal that stays refrigerated and only needs a short reheating. It contains cooked pasta, a creamy sauce made from cream and cheese, and a mix of seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid). The dish balances a smooth dairy flavor with a distinct marine taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often prepared with a blend of heavy cream and Parmesan, giving it a velvety texture.
Seafood is usually sautéed beforehand to preserve its aroma and tenderness.
Vacuum‑sealed ready meals stay fresh for up to 7 days when kept in the fridge.
Hard‑grain pastas such as penne or fettuccine are preferred because they hold the sauce better.
Microwave reheating typically takes 2–3 minutes, but stirring halfway ensures even heating.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid) provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood supplies omega‑3s, which support heart and vascular health.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The creamy sauce and cheese deliver calcium, while seafood adds vitamin D, both important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains B12 and B6, which help maintain normal nervous system function.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Pasta provides quick‑release carbohydrates, useful for replenishing energy after physical activity.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: People allergic to shrimp, mussels or squid may experience severe reactions when consuming this product.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The cream sauce makes the dish calorie‑dense; those watching weight should control portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Ready‑made meals often contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Thermal treatment
items.content: Insufficient reheating can leave cold spots where bacteria may survive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave (or on the stovetop) until steaming hot, stirring halfway to ensure even temperature. For extra flavor, garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in the original packaging. Once opened, consume within 3‑4 days. If frozen, the product can be stored up to 2 months, though pasta texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard coated pretzels are a baked snack made from wheat flour, shaped into the classic knot and finished with a salty or sweet coating. They belong to the snack category and are usually sold in 30‑50 g packages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional German pretzel shape symbolizes the crossed arms of monks.
Hard pretzels first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient travel snack.
Coatings can be salty or sweet (chocolate, caramel, glaze).
In Japan, small versions coated with soy sauce and sea salt are popular.
The NFS code (3021) is used in the company's internal inventory system to identify the product.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Hard pretzels contain starch, providing sustained satiety.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Wheat flour provides a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: Vitamin B1 content
items.content: Thiamine, especially in whole‑grain versions, supports nervous system function.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, hard pretzels have little fat unless a buttery glaze is added.

items.title: Convenient energy source
items.content: Readily digestible carbs make them a good pre‑exercise or on‑the‑go snack.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Salty coatings can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The product contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar in sweet coatings
items.content: Sweet varieties may contain added sugars, which are undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The hard texture can pose a choking risk for young children; supervision is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed straight from the pack, added to salads, used as a base for cheese spreads, or broken and seasoned with spices. Sweet‑coated pretzels are often served with ice cream or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight container. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain crispness. Avoid moisture, which will make pretzels soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Relish is a pickled cucumber seasoned with spices, vinegar, and sugar. It has a sweet‑sour flavor, crisp texture, and a strong aroma. Relish is commonly used as a garnish, sandwich topping, salad addition, or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickling cucumbers dates back over 4,000 years and appears in many cultures.
The combination of vinegar, sugar, and spices allows the cucumbers to be preserved for several months.
Typical relish spices include dill, mustard seeds, black pepper, and garlic, giving it a distinctive scent.
Relish can be made sweet or spicy depending on the ingredient ratios.
In some countries relish is served in small cubes, while in others it is sliced into larger pieces.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation of cucumbers creates beneficial bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Cucumbers are low in calories, and the pickling process adds minimal fat.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Cucumbers provide vitamin K, important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Spices and vinegar contribute antioxidant compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Cucumbers are over 90 % water, aiding the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickling requires a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Acidic vinegar
items.content: Vinegar’s acidity can irritate the stomach in individuals with sensitivity.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may react to mustard, dill, or garlic used in relish.

items.title: Bacterial risk if stored improperly
items.content: If kept above 4 °C for extended periods, unwanted microbes can grow.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add relish to burgers, sandwiches, salads, snacks, and cheese plates. It also works as a side for meat dishes or a tangy accompaniment to beer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store relish in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed jar. Properly stored, it retains its flavor for 3‑4 months. Discard if you notice mold, off‑smell, or color changes.

tea-iced-brewed-green-decaffeinated-unsw.title: Tea, Iced, Brewed, Green, Decaffeinated, Unsweetened

content.title: About
content.content: Iced brewed green tea that is decaffeinated and unsweetened is a refreshing beverage made from Camellia sinensis leaves that have undergone caffeine removal and cold‑brew extraction. It retains the grassy flavor of green tea while containing no caffeine or added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is rich in polyphenols, especially epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), known for strong antioxidant activity.
Decaffeination is usually performed with solvents or super‑critical CO₂, preserving most flavor compounds.
Cold‑brew extraction occurs at 4‑10 °C for 6‑12 hours, resulting in a smoother, less bitter taste.
Because it is unsweetened, this tea is often used as a base for smoothies, mocktails, and flavored drinks.
In Japan, similar unsweetened cold green teas are served as “mucha” (cold tea without added sugar).

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and catechins help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Regular green tea consumption is linked to improved lipid profiles and lower blood pressure.

items.title: Promotes relaxation
items.content: L‑theanine in green tea encourages calmness without drowsiness.

items.title: Aids weight management
items.content: A low‑calorie, sugar‑free drink can replace higher‑calorie beverages, supporting a calorie deficit.

items.title: Oral health support
items.content: Catechins have antibacterial properties that reduce plaque‑forming bacteria.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High catechin levels can affect the metabolism of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

items.title: Fluoride content
items.content: Tea can contain fluoride; excessive intake may affect teeth and bones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the iced green tea plain, or add lemon slices, mint, or berries for extra flavor. It works well as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails, smoothies, or as a culinary ingredient in marinades for fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared beverage in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑5 days. Store dry tea leaves in a cool, dry, dark place in an airtight package.
